identification.summary: Mofang is a cyber-espionage group that Dutch security firm Fox-IT named and publicly exposed in June 2016. Fox-IT assesses it as almost certainly operating out of China and probably government-affiliated [S1][S2]. MITRE ATT&CK describes it as a likely China-based group that has run focused attacks on government and critical infrastructure in Myanmar and other countries, and says the name comes from its frequent practice of imitating a victim's infrastructure [S4]. The group relies on social engineering rather than exploits, delivering its custom ShimRat and ShimRatReporter tools [S1][S2][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Fox-IT reporting (via SecurityWeek): active since at least February 2012 [S2]. MITRE ATT&CK: observed since at least May 2012 [S4]. Fox-IT published its report on 2016-06-15 [S1].
identification.notes: MITRE ATT&CK group ID G0103 [S4]. The imported record lists BRONZE WALKER (Secureworks CTU) and Superman as aliases, but no cited source in this file confirms either name, so neither is added to aliasesAdd. Start dates differ: February 2012 in Fox-IT-derived press coverage [S2] versus May 2012 in MITRE [S4].

attribution.sponsor: Suspected People's Republic of China government affiliation (vendor assessment only) [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Fox-IT says the actor almost certainly operates out of China and is probably government-affiliated [S1][S2]. MITRE describes it as a likely China-based group [S4]. These are vendor and knowledge-base assessments, not government attribution; no US or allied government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Fox-IT's analysis of tooling, infrastructure and target selection, which it links to investments or technological advances that could threaten the Chinese sphere of influence [S1][S2]. Press coverage reports that targeting of the Myanmar Kyaukphyu special economic zone lined up in time with a tender later won by China's CITIC group [S2].

objectives: Politically and economically motivated information theft. Fox-IT links Mofang's target selection to investments or technological advances that could be perceived as a threat to China's sphere of influence [S1]. Press reporting says experts believe information taken from Myanmar government organizations and the Singapore firm CPG Corporation could have helped a Chinese company win the Kyaukphyu infrastructure tender. This is an expert inference, not a confirmed outcome [S2].

sectors: Engineering and consulting firms involved in Myanmar infrastructure (CPG Corporation) [S2]
targeting.notes: Fox-IT suspects there are more victims than the countries it lists [S1]. In 2015-2016 the reported targeting centers on Myanmar and on organizations with interests in Myanmar's Kyaukphyu special economic zone [S2].

capabilities.summary: Mofang does not use exploits for initial infection. It relies on social engineering, usually email inviting targets to open attached files or follow links [S1][S2]. The only exploits reported in its toolset are previously known privilege-escalation exploits built into the malware [S2]. Its custom tools ShimRat (a remote access trojan) and ShimRatReporter (used for automated initial discovery) date back to at least 2012 [S2][S4]. MITRE lists two software entries for the group, ShimRat (S0444) and ShimRatReporter (S0445). It also lists spearphishing attachments and links, user execution, and encrypted or compressed payloads among the group's techniques [S4]. The group's name comes from its practice of imitating victim infrastructure, such as lookalike domains [S4].

campaigns.name: Early ShimRat operations
campaigns.summary: Mofang has been active since at least February 2012 (MITRE: May 2012), targeting government, military, critical infrastructure, automotive and weapons organizations in several countries including India, Germany, Canada, the United States, Singapore and South Korea [S2][S4].

campaigns.name: Kyaukphyu special economic zone targeting
campaigns.summary: In mid-2015 Mofang attacked Myanmar government organizations and the Singapore-based firm CPG Corporation, which had won a 2014 consulting tender for the Kyaukphyu SEZ. CITIC was later declared winner of an infrastructure tender in early 2016. Experts believe stolen information could have helped the Chinese bidder, though this is not confirmed [S2].

campaigns.name: Fox-IT public exposure
campaigns.summary: Fox-IT published its Mofang threat report, describing the group as almost certainly China-based and probably government-affiliated [S1][S3].

diamond.adversary: A likely China-based espionage group that Fox-IT assesses as probably government-affiliated [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Social-engineering lures carrying the custom ShimRat RAT and ShimRatReporter discovery tool. The malware has built-in, previously known privilege-escalation exploits, and payloads are encrypted or compressed [S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Infrastructure that imitates the victim's own, which is the source of the 'Mofang' name [S4]. Specific domains and IP addresses are in the Fox-IT report, which was not opened for this file.
diamond.victim: Myanmar government and organizations tied to the Kyaukphyu SEZ (for example CPG Corporation), plus government, military, critical infrastructure, automotive and weapons organizations in India, Germany, the United States, Canada, Singapore and South Korea [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Targeting tracks Chinese strategic and economic interests, such as Myanmar's Kyaukphyu SEZ, where China's CNPC had invested and CITIC won an infrastructure tender [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints reached through email and user execution of attachments or links [S2][S4].

gaps: The Fox-IT blog and the full Fox-IT PDF report (foxitsecurity.files.wordpress.com) could not be opened, because WebFetch failed on DNS for all hosts. Facts come from search-result excerpts and press coverage.
No source returned in search confirms the BRONZE WALKER (Secureworks CTU) alias. The Secureworks threat profile URL in the record was not retrievable.
The 'Superman' alias appears in Rapid7 InsightIDR documentation (docs.rapid7.com/insightidr/mofang/), which has no visible date. It was not added to aliasesAdd.

Secondary reports (an ESMT Digital Society Institute blog post, and Bright.nl citing De Volkskrant) name Rheinmetall as a German victim. They also say that from early 2015 Myanmar organizations were the only victims. These sources are undated in the search results and unverified.
There is no public reporting on Mofang activity after 2016. Whether the group is still active, was renamed, or merged into another cluster is unknown.
The CFR Cyber Operations Tracker entry for Mofang could not be retrieved.
No government (US or allied) attribution or indictment was found. Attribution rests on Fox-IT and MITRE assessments.
Specific indicators (domains, C2 IPs, hashes) and details of ShimRat's application-shimming persistence were not verified from primary sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1 (operational environment): concern centers on organizations tied to Chinese strategic investments and infrastructure projects, especially in Myanmar and South/Southeast Asia, and on defense and weapons-industry partners in allied nations [S1][S2]. Step 2 (effects): exposure is mainly loss of confidentiality of negotiating positions, tender data and defense-industrial information. No destructive activity is reported [S1][S2]. Step 3 (threat evaluation): low-sophistication initial access through social engineering, with no exploit-based entry; custom ShimRat tooling; and infrastructure that imitates victims [S2][S4]. Step 4: MLCOA is spearphishing with attachments or links aimed at government and partner organizations involved in China-linked economic projects, followed by ShimRat discovery and data theft [S2][S4]. MDCOA is long-term access to defense-industrial or military networks in partner nations, exposing weapons or program data [S2]. Candidate indicators include lookalike domains that mimic the victim organization [S4], email attachments that drop compressed or encrypted payloads [S4], and unexpected shim database installation (inferred from the ShimRat name; validate).
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Mofang's reported activity is from 2012-2016, with no recent public reporting, so treat it as a historical case study of economically motivated PRC-linked espionage rather than a current tracked threat [S1][S2][S4]. Authorities: attribution is vendor-only (Fox-IT, MITRE), so any defensive action should rest on observed indicators rather than government attribution [S1][S4]. Mission assurance: the threat to deployed or partner-nation networks comes mainly from user-targeted phishing, so user awareness and email and attachment controls are the main mitigations [S1][S2]. Coordination: the targeting of partner governments (for example Myanmar) and defense industry in allied countries [S2] suggests information sharing with partners and the defense industrial base.
